17 active human trafficking cases recorded by Police, concerns raised over unreported incidents
item.description: Navitalai Naivalurua · 21/11/2026 The Fiji Police Force has 17 active human trafficking cases between 2020 and 2026, with nine pending investigation and eight being referred to the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP) for independent review.
item.content:encoded:
Navitalai Naivalurua · 21/11/2026

The Fiji Police Force has 17 active human trafficking cases between 2020 and 2026, with nine pending investigation and eight being referred to the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP) for independent review.

This was revealed by Assistant Commissioner of Police Crime Loraini Seru during the 2026 Annual ODPP Conference at Shangri-La Fiji Resort , where she also raised concerns about unreported cases highlighted in the 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report for Fiji.

She says the cases are being investigated by the Force's Human Trafficking Unit.

The Assistant Commissioner says that, with Fiji's total population standing at around 935,000, one of the biggest challenges they continue to face is the issue of unreported cases, despite information being available.

She adds that while police and other law enforcement agencies may have intelligence information, some incidents have not been formally reported.

item.title: People have lost trust in the Constitution Bill process – Prof. Prasad
item.description: The majority of people in Fiji have lost trust in the process being followed for the Constitution Amendment Bill. National Federation Party Leader Professor Biman Â Prasad highlighted this during fijivillage Straight Talk with Vijay Narayan when asked why the NFP is not supporting the third reading of the Bill.
item.content:encoded:
The majority of people in Fiji have lost trust in the process being followed for the Constitution Amendment Bill.

National Federation Party Leader Professor Biman Â Prasad highlighted this during fijivillage Straight Talk with Vijay Narayan when asked why the NFP is not supporting the third reading of the Bill.

He says the NFP cannot support the process, the implementation of the proposed constitutional changes or the third reading of the Bill because the party believes people have lost trust, and it cannot betray them.

He makes it clear that being part of a coalition government does not prevent individual parties from taking different positions on important national issues.

The NFP Leader says the party publicly identified 18 issues in the Cabinet Subcommittee's draft bill that needed attention.

He says the problems began with the draft bill itself, including errors, the proposal to recognise Christianity as a founding value and departures from the Constitution Review Commission's draft.

Professor Prasad says these issues created alarm and concern among the people.

He further says that although consultations were held, there was insufficient interaction with the public and little opportunity to properly explain many of the proposed provisions.

Professor Prasad says constitutional changes must have legitimacy and acceptance from the people, but he believes there is not enough time to achieve this.

Professor Prasad adds that the process should be left until after the next general election, while the Government focuses on more pressing issues.

Meanwhile, Deputy Party Leader Lenora Qereqeretabua says the 2013 Constitution was imposed on the people, and Fijians do not want another imposed constitution.

Qereqeretabua questioned the urgency of the proposed amendments, saying the process should be delayed until after the elections.

She says there are many more important priorities that need to be addressed, including drought, with people having to choose between providing water for their animals and other essential needs.

She adds that boreholes which were promised have yet to be dug.

The Deputy Party Leader says Fiji is also approaching the cyclone season, and she questioned if the country is prepared.

Qereqeretabua says there needs to be a much deeper conversation about the proposed amendments, and the first step should be to translate the Constitution Amendment Bill into languages that everyone can understand.

She adds that the consultation process has been conducted in English, with insufficient time given to submitters to express their views and concerns.

item.title: El Niño-affected communities to be prioritised for water tank assistance
item.description: Communities affected by El Niño will be prioritised for water tanks under a new assistance programme by the Ministry of Multi-Ethnic Affairs, with applications now open for the next two weeks. Permanent Secretary for Multi-Ethnic Affairs Dr Vinesh Kumar says the Ministry introduced the Community Resilience Programme after identifying water storage and management as one of the biggest challenges fa
item.content:encoded:
Communities affected by El Niño will be prioritised for water tanks under a new assistance programme by the Ministry of Multi-Ethnic Affairs, with applications now open for the next two weeks.

Permanent Secretary for Multi-Ethnic Affairs Dr Vinesh Kumar says the Ministry introduced the Community Resilience Programme after identifying water storage and management as one of the biggest challenges facing communities during its ground assessments.

Kumar says although agencies have been providing water to affected communities, storing it and distributing it safely has remained a challenge.

He says the programme will prioritise communal water tanks to help communities manage their water resources.

Kumar says applications opened on Wednesday 18th November and will remain open for two weeks.

He says the Ministry has simplified the application process to ensure affected families and communities can access assistance without going through a lengthy process.

Kumar says the Ministry will assess applications as they come in and will not wait until the application period closes before providing assistance.

He says the Western and Northern divisions are among the priority areas, although communities affected in the Central and Eastern divisions can also apply.

Kumar says the Ministry will work with the Rural and Maritime Development Ministry, the National Disaster Risk Management Office and the Water Authority of Fiji to ensure assistance complements existing efforts and does not duplicate resources.

He says applications will be verified and endorsed through district officers, provincial administrators or commissioners' offices to ensure assistance reaches communities that need it most.

On borehole projects, Kumar says the Ministry completed five borehole projects and eight water management projects in the 2024-2025 financial year.

He says in the 2025-2026 financial year, the Ministry had 18 borehole projects and commissioned six water management projects.

Kumar says 45 borehole applications are currently undergoing verification in the Western Division, with further requests also received from the Northern Division.

He says the projects are community-based and the Ministry is working to expedite the verification process so communities do not have to wait too long for assistance.

Kumar says the Ministry is also exploring a possible partnership with an NGO based in Labasa to support borehole projects in communities.

He says the Ministry is currently working within its existing budget allocation but is exploring further funding opportunities.

Kumar says carrying out borehole projects in some areas, particularly in the Northern Division, can be challenging because machinery and other resources have to be mobilised.
